translations: Taiwan's tech industry lacked a substantial domestic market, so its downstream customers were overseas. To understand market needs, Taiwan's personal computer industry had to go abroad and then relay those insights back to the island's semiconductor sector—arriving, of course, one step late. Conversely, if Taiwan's semiconductor industry could produce cutting-edge products, should it seek out foreign computer companies with close contact with the market, or turn to the Taiwan computer industry separated from it? The answer was obvious: the foreign companies.
The absence of a large home market—and with it, the mechanism for close upstream-downstream integration—was a major obstacle to sustained growth in the tech industry.

More than a decade ago, compensation for Taiwan's tech workers lagged far behind that of their American counterparts. Today most have reached parity, and a few exceed it. With rising incomes, expectations for life itself began to change. A dozen years ago, the tree-lined workplaces of the Hsinchu Science Park were considered remarkably beautiful, almost rare; now most regarded them as merely standard. Back then, the employee dormitories in Hsinchu were considered luxurious; today most found them substandard. Pollution, noise, traffic congestion—phenomena that had been either mild or unnoticed not long ago—now provoked serious dissatisfaction, complaints rising everywhere inside and outside the park.

Beyond the material dimensions of quality of life stood its cultural ones: public safety, social justice, an honest government, the curbing of the influence of moneyed interests. Perhaps these problems were less acute before, or more tolerated; but now dissatisfaction had not only intensified, people came to see them universally as a poison corroding Taiwan's overall competitiveness.

The United States remained a magnet drawing talent from around the world. Many successful Chinese-American professionals had rooted themselves there, and Taiwanese students who went to study in the U.S. increasingly chose not to return. Why did America still hold such pull? Pay differentials alone could no longer explain it. The main reason was the quality of life—the material and cultural life—America offered.

Taiwanese culture possessed many strengths that had propelled its tech industry to its present achievement: a deep reverence for education, industry, professional dedication. Yet in recent years these virtues seemed to be fading. In their place, corrosive habits had taken root—greed, short-sightedness, speculation, the pursuit of shortcuts. Worse, they carried the force of Gresham's Law, driving out the better sort. Unless reversed, Taiwanese society risked becoming one where decent people held back and refused to advance—a condition wholly incompatible with sustained high-tech development. What was needed was a large number of people with a sense of mission…
